results.result: The intercalated cushions (IC) develop as distinct morphological structures within the outflow tract wall between E9.5 and E15.5 in mouse embryos, with similar patterns observed in human embryos. At E9.5, no discrete cushions are evident, but by E10.5 the IC appear as thickenings in the outflow tract wall. By E11.5-E12.5, the IC become compact swellings that appear morphologically similar to the main cushions, though with denser cell packing. The aortic and pulmonary IC differ in their positioning and relationship to surrounding myocardium.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C32 provide a detailed temporal and spatial description of IC development supported by histological observations across multiple developmental stages (E9.5-E15.5) in both mouse and human embryos. The observations are internally consistent and supported by multiple figures (Figure 1C-R). The morphological descriptions are appropriately qualified (e.g., 'appeared more dense') and the comparative observations between aortic and pulmonary IC are well-documented.

results.result: The IC undergo late differentiation to become valve primordia, characterized by delayed expression of valve markers compared to main cushions. At E10.5, the IC lack CS56 and cTnI expression but are overlaid by a thin layer of CS56-expressing cardiac jelly. Versican and Sox9 expression appear in the IC by E11.5, prior to CS56 expression at E12.5. This temporal pattern indicates that early-stage IC are not classical endocardial cushions but mature to express valve interstitial cell markers.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C47 describe a coherent temporal sequence of marker expression supported by immunohistochemistry data (Figure 2). The progression from CS56-negative (E10.5) to Versican-positive (E11.5) to CS56-positive (E12.5) is well-documented. The inference that IC are not classical endocardial cushions (C46) is appropriately drawn from the marker expression patterns. Multiple technical replicates (n≥3) strengthen the observations.

results.result: Neural crest cells (NCC) and endothelial-derived cells (EDC) make major contributions to the main outflow cushions but only minor contributions to the IC. Statistical analysis shows significant differences in Wnt1-Cre+ and Tek-Cre+ lineage cell proportions between valve primordia (p<0.0001). The aortic posterior and pulmonary anterior primordia have significantly fewer NCC than other primordia. Epicardially-derived cells do not contribute to arterial valve leaflets.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C54 are supported by quantitative cell counting data with appropriate statistical analysis (chi-squared tests with Bonferroni correction, n>6800 cells). The statistical significance is properly reported with p-values and degrees of freedom. The negative result for epicardial contribution (C54) is clearly documented. The data build on prior work (Phillips et al., 2013) with more thorough quantitative analysis.

results.result: Cells derived from Mef2c-AHF-Cre+ second heart field (SHF) make major and reproducible contributions to all arterial valve leaflet primordia, including the IC. Statistical analysis shows significant differences in Mef2c-AHF-Cre+ cell proportions between primordia (p<0.0001). Importantly, the distribution of Mef2c-AHF-Cre+ cells is complementary to Wnt1-Cre+ lineage cells and sufficient to account for all cells in the valve primordia.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C57 are supported by quantitative lineage tracing data (n=7435 cells) with appropriate statistical analysis. The complementary distribution between Mef2c-AHF-Cre+ and Wnt1-Cre+ lineages (C57) is a critical finding supported by direct comparison of cell counts (Figure 3J vs 3E). The reproducibility is noted and the sample sizes are adequate for the statistical tests performed.

results.result: The IC and adjacent outflow tract wall are composed of Tnnt2-Cre+ lineage cells that do not express differentiated cardiomyocyte markers (cTnT, cTnI, αSMA) at any developmental stage examined. Tnnt2-Cre+/cTnT- cells are present as early as E9.75, before IC formation. These cells contribute to valve leaflets throughout gestation and postnatally, but the data argue against trans-differentiation from cardiomyocytes.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C66 are supported by lineage tracing combined with immunohistochemistry at multiple developmental stages (E9.75-postnatal). The critical observation that Tnnt2-Cre+ cells never co-express cardiomyocyte markers (C63) is well-documented across multiple time points. The inference against trans-differentiation (C66) is appropriately drawn from the absence of co-expression at any stage examined. The temporal analysis is thorough.

results.result: Cre protein expression analysis reveals that Tnnt2-Cre is activated in the forming IC at E10.5 but is absent by E11.5-E12.5, while remaining in myocardial walls. Taking into account Cre protein perdurance, activation likely occurs before E10.5, prior to full cardiomyocyte differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C69 are supported by anti-Cre antibody staining (Figure 3—figure supplement 2). The temporal pattern of Cre protein expression provides important mechanistic insight into the timing of Tnnt2 promoter activation. The inference about timing (C69) appropriately considers Cre protein stability. This addresses a potential concern about the interpretation of lineage tracing data.

results.result: Tnnt2-Cre+ lineage cells are observed in smooth muscle cells (SMC) within the arterial wall at later developmental stages.
results.evaluation: Claim C70 is supported by observations shown in Figure 3N and Figure 3—figure supplement 3. This finding is noted as interesting and suggests broader implications for SHF contributions, though detailed characterization is noted as beyond the scope of the manuscript.

results.result: The IC are delineated by Isl1 expression at E11.5, with some cells co-expressing Sox9, indicating direct differentiation into valve interstitial cells. Isl1 expression is maintained longer in IC cells than surrounding cells and essentially disappears by E12.5. The concomitant reduction of Isl1 and increase in Sox9, without expression of differentiated cardiomyocyte markers, supports direct derivation from SHF progenitors rather than trans-differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C75 are supported by immunofluorescence data showing Isl1 and Sox9 co-expression (Figure 3W-Y, Figure 3—figure supplement 4). The temporal pattern of marker expression provides strong evidence for direct differentiation. The inference (C75) is appropriately drawn from the marker expression patterns and absence of differentiated markers. The logic is sound and well-supported.

results.result: The IC express epithelial markers (E-cadherin, β-catenin, laminin) at E10.5 that are progressively downregulated by E11.5-E12.5, but do not express typical mesenchymal markers (N-cadherin, Fsp1). Collagen I and elastin are transiently expressed specifically in IC at E11.5. This pattern suggests epithelial SHF progenitors differentiate to valve interstitial cells without passing through an undifferentiated mesenchymal intermediate.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C84 are supported by comprehensive immunofluorescence analysis of epithelial and mesenchymal markers (Figure 4A-R). The temporal progression of marker expression is well-documented. The absence of mesenchymal markers (C79) is clearly shown. The inference about direct differentiation without a mesenchymal intermediate (C84) is appropriately drawn from the marker expression patterns, though this is a significant departure from conventional models.

results.result: Slug and Snail transcripts are not expressed in the IC at E10.5 or E11.5, although both are abundantly expressed in the endothelium and mesenchyme of main outflow cushions. This indicates that IC cells do not undergo classical epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) despite changing from epithelial to valve interstitial cell phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C86 are supported by in situ hybridization data (Figure 4S-V, Figure 4—figure supplement 1). The absence of Slug and Snail expression in IC contrasts with their presence in main cushions, providing strong evidence against classical EMT. The inference (C86) is appropriately drawn. This is a critical mechanistic finding that challenges conventional understanding of valve development.

results.result: Notch signaling components show specific temporal and spatial expression in the IC. Active Notch1 (N1ICD) is expressed in IC at E10.5 but only in a few overlying cells by E11.5. Notch2, Jag1, and Jag2 are expressed in IC, with Jag1 in the core and Jag2 in the adluminal region. By E12.5, these components are absent from IC interstitial cells but present in endothelium. This pattern suggests Notch signaling is temporally and spatially associated with IC differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C102 are supported by detailed immunofluorescence analysis of Notch pathway components (Figure 5). The temporal window of expression (E10.5-E11.5) and spatial patterns are well-documented. The differential localization of Jag1 vs Jag2 (C96-C97) is clearly shown. The co-localization studies with Isl1 (C98-C99) provide additional mechanistic insight. The inference about association with differentiation (C102) is appropriately drawn.

results.result: Genetic deletion experiments show that single deletion of Jag1 or Jag2 using Tnnt2-Cre does not cause bicuspid aortic valve (BAV), but combined deletion results in BAV in 4/11 embryos and dysplastic leaflets in an additional 4/11 embryos. The posterior (non-coronary) leaflet is specifically affected, appearing absent without evidence of raphe. Most valve defects (7/9) occur with other cardiac anomalies.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C110 are supported by genetic experiments with appropriate controls and quantification (Figure 6A-D). The redundancy between Jag1 and Jag2 is demonstrated by the requirement for double deletion to produce phenotypes. The specific loss of the posterior leaflet (C106) is well-documented. The penetrance (4/11 for BAV, 9/11 total abnormalities) is clearly reported. The association with other cardiac defects (C110) is noted, though this raises questions about specificity.

results.result: Mib1f/f;Tnnt2-Cre embryos show absence (1/9) or dysplasia (8/9) of the non-coronary leaflet at E16.5. At E11.5, the IC are poorly formed with fewer Sox9+/Isl1+ cells in 1/3 of mutants examined. This supports a critical role for Notch signaling in IC formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C113 are supported by analysis of Mib1 mutants (Figure 6E-H), confirming prior findings (Captur et al., 2016). The examination of IC formation at E11.5 (C112) provides mechanistic insight linking the valve defects to IC development. The inference about Notch signaling's role (C113) is appropriately drawn. The penetrance is clearly reported.

results.result: SHF addition to the outflow tract wall is required for IC formation, which give rise to the posterior leaflet of the aortic valve and the anterior leaflet of the pulmonary valve.
results.evaluation: Claim C114 synthesizes findings from lineage tracing and genetic deletion experiments. The requirement for SHF is demonstrated by Vangl2 and Tbx1 mutant phenotypes. The specific leaflet identities are supported by positional and lineage tracing data. This is an appropriate inference from the collective data.

results.result: Vangl2f/f;Isl1-Cre embryos show dysplastic leaflets and BAV without raphe in 57% (4/7) at E15.5, with absence of the posterior leaflet. At E10.5-E11.5, the IC are present but misplaced and smaller in 2/6 cases. Despite apparently normal expression of Isl1, β-catenin, and E-cadherin, Notch1ICD and Jag1 are reduced in 2/3 embryos, and there is abnormal distribution of cTnI-expressing cells. This suggests IC may be mis-specified or prematurely differentiate to myocardium.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C123 are supported by analysis of Vangl2 mutants (Figure 7). The BAV phenotype is well-documented with clear penetrance (4/7). The IC abnormalities at earlier stages (C118-C119) provide mechanistic insight. The reduction in Notch signaling components (C121) suggests a potential mechanism. The inference about mis-specification (C123) is appropriately qualified as a suggestion. The sample sizes are adequate for the descriptive observations.

results.result: Tbx1-/- embryos show markedly abnormal valve leaflets within the unseptated outflow tract at E15.5 and E12.5. A single IC is visible at E12.5, and at E11.5 a well-developed aortic IC is present but a discrete pulmonary IC cannot be distinguished. This suggests disrupted IC development may underpin arterial valve defects in Tbx1 mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C127 are supported by analysis of Tbx1 null mice (Figure 8). The observations are clearly documented with appropriate staging. The specific loss of the pulmonary IC (C126) while the aortic IC is preserved provides important insight into differential regulation. The inference (C127) is appropriately qualified. This extends prior observations on Tbx1 mutants to focus on IC development.

results.result: Arterial valve formation differs from atrioventricular valves due to large NCC influx and dominant SHF role. The central four leaflets are filled by NCC and SHF cells via EndMT, while the intercalated valve structures differentiate directly from Mef2c-AHF-Cre+;Tnnt2-Cre+ SHF-derived outflow wall. These cells retain cardiac troponin promoter activation signatures but are not myocardial. They mature by expressing Sox9 and Versican without EndMT or typical mesenchymal markers, ultimately appearing indistinguishable from main cushion-derived leaflets.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C133 synthesize the major findings of the study. The distinction between central leaflets (via EndMT) and intercalated leaflets (direct differentiation) is supported by the lineage tracing, marker expression, and genetic data presented. The characterization of the Tnnt2-Cre+ population (C131) is well-supported. The ultimate similarity of mature leaflets (C133) is documented. This represents an appropriate high-level summary of the work.

results.result: Three lineages contribute to arterial valve leaflets: NCC, endothelial-derived cells (EDC), and a novel SHF progenitor population that transiently activates Tnnt2-Cre but differentiates directly to valve interstitial cells. This novel population makes the major contribution to anterior/posterior leaflets from IC and significant contributions to left/right leaflets. There is no evidence of trans-differentiation from cardiomyocytes or SMC; instead, concomitant reduction of Isl1 and increase in Sox9 indicates direct differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C138 synthesize the lineage tracing and marker expression data to define a novel cell population. The three-lineage model (C136) is supported by the quantitative cell counting showing complementary distributions. The specific contributions to different leaflets (C137) are well-documented. The evidence against trans-differentiation (C138) is strong, based on absence of co-expression at all stages examined. This is a major conceptual advance.

results.result: Tnnt2-Cre+ lineage cells contribute to postnatal valve leaflets. Transient Tnnt2 promoter activation likely occurred in undifferentiated SHF progenitors within the distal outflow, as cTnT protein was never detected. These cells activated Sox9 and differentiated to valve interstitial cells at E11.5, approximately one day later than proximal cells differentiated to cardiomyocytes. The delay in differentiation may explain Tnnt2 promoter activation in cells poised but stalled for differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C141 are supported by the lineage tracing and marker expression data. The inference about undifferentiated progenitors (C140) is appropriately drawn from the absence of cTnT protein. The temporal delay in differentiation (C141) is documented. The speculation about the mechanism (C142) is appropriately qualified and represents a reasonable hypothesis based on the data.

results.result: The Tnnt2-Cre+ lineage in IC provides a tool to investigate IC development genes, allowing deletion in directly-differentiating SHF without affecting NCC or EDC. The arterial valve defects in Mib1;Tnnt2-Cre mutants likely arise from Tnnt2-Cre activation in valve primordia, deleting Mib1 and inactivating Jag1/Jag2-Notch signaling.
results.evaluation: Claim C143 is a reasonable inference about the utility of the Tnnt2-Cre line, supported by the specificity demonstrated in the lineage tracing experiments. Claim C144 provides a mechanistic explanation for the Mib1 mutant phenotype, appropriately linking the Cre expression pattern to the genetic deletion and resulting phenotype. Both are appropriately qualified inferences.

results.result: EndMT is crucial for typical endocardial cushions but not for IC, where the major process is direct differentiation from SHF cells in situ. There is minor ECM deposition and Sox9+ cells in the sub-endothelial compartment of IC, indicating a small EndMT contribution. Evidence from Brg1 knockout in endothelium using Nfatc1-Cre shows both anterior and posterior leaflets are well-formed, supporting that IC are not dependent on EndMT.
results.evaluation: Claims C145-C146 are supported by the marker expression data showing absence of EndMT markers in the bulk of IC. The acknowledgment of minor EndMT contribution (C146) is appropriate given the Sox9+ cells near the endothelium. Claim C147 cites external evidence (Akerberg et al., 2015) that supports the conclusion, though the authors did not generate this data themselves. The integration of external evidence is appropriate.

results.result: IC form as expansions of compacted cells within the distal outflow tract wall from cells continuous with epithelial SHF. These condensations form at the proximal extent of the non-myocardial distal outflow wall, likely reflecting asymmetrical SHF addition and outflow wall rotation. IC cells appear to share an origin with and be juxtaposed to the myocardial component, with both populations being Tnnt2-Cre+, suggesting a close relationship.
results.evaluation: Claims C148-C151 synthesize morphological observations with lineage tracing data. The description of IC formation (C148) is supported by the histological data and agrees with prior work (Sizarov et al., 2012). The relationship to the 'fishmouth' structure (C149) is documented in Figure 1O. The shared Tnnt2-Cre+ lineage (C151) is well-established. These are appropriate inferences from the data.

results.result: Jag1 is abundantly expressed in IC (which do not use EndMT/EMT) and outflow tract myocardium. Notch1 and/or Notch2 are likely the main receptors in IC. The presence and subsequent removal of Notch1 signaling may be essential for IC differentiation to valve interstitial cells. Jag1 and Jag2 show redundancy reminiscent of ventricular development, though Jag2 is restricted to adluminal cells while Jag1 is in the core, suggesting ligand-specific functional specialization.
results.evaluation: Claims C152-C156 synthesize the Notch pathway expression data with functional genetic experiments. The expression patterns (C152) are well-documented. The inference about receptors (C153) is appropriately qualified and supported by the expression data and cited literature. The speculation about signaling dynamics (C154) is appropriately qualified. The redundancy (C155) is demonstrated by the genetic experiments. The differential localization (C156) is clearly shown and the inference about specialization is reasonable.

results.result: Vangl2;Isl1-Cre and Tbx1 mutants, both with limited SHF addition to outflow, have abnormal valve leaflets from failure to form or mature IC. In Vangl2 mutants, premature SHF differentiation to cardiomyocytes may reduce availability of cells to form Sox9+ valve interstitial cells, leading to reduced IC size and BAV. Reduced Notch1ICD and Jag1 suggest Notch signaling may be regulated by Vangl2. Defects are more common in aortic valve, and the SHF contributing to aorta is preferentially affected.
results.evaluation: Claims C157-C162 synthesize observations from two mutant models to propose a common mechanism. The IC defects in both models (C157) are well-documented. The proposed mechanism for Vangl2 (C158) is a reasonable inference based on prior work (Ramsbottom et al., 2014) and current observations. The link to Notch signaling (C159) is supported by the expression data, though the mechanism is appropriately qualified. The aortic preference (C160-C162) is documented and the inference about SHF subdomains is reasonable.

results.result: Premature loss of progenitor phenotype and cardiomyocyte differentiation leading to reduced SHF-derived subpulmonary myocardium has been reported in Tbx1 mutants, as has absence of the anterior pulmonary valve leaflet. The role of both Vangl2 and Tbx1 in regulating SHF epithelial properties suggests this phenotype may be crucial. This raises the possibility of an intrinsic relationship between loss of epithelial properties and cardiomyocyte differentiation. Differences between affected valves in Vangl2 vs Tbx1 mutants likely reflect outflow tract patterning differences and SHF subdomains.
results.evaluation: Claims C163-C167 integrate current findings with prior literature. The cited observations (C163-C164) are appropriately referenced. The inference about epithelial properties (C165) is supported by the E-cadherin expression data and cited work. The speculation about epithelial-differentiation relationships (C166) is appropriately qualified. The explanation for differences between mutants (C167) is a reasonable inference supported by cited literature on SHF patterning.

results.result: BAV has been described in multiple mouse mutants, with several cases showing specific failure of anterior/non-coronary leaflets to form properly. This may be a common mechanism underlying BAV without raphe formation in mice, occurring with SHF disruption. Human and mouse valve primordia appearances and Isl1 expression patterns are very similar at comparable stages. Loss of SHF progenitors may be a common cause of BAV and explain associations with other cardiac malformations. This may link to the 5-10% of BAV cases without raphe. Genomic analysis of such patients should focus on SHF and Jag-Notch pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C168-C173 appropriately synthesize current findings with literature to propose broader implications. The cited examples (C169) support the generality of the mechanism. The human-mouse similarity (C171) is documented in Figure 1I-L. The proposed common mechanism (C172) is a reasonable inference. The link to human BAV subtypes (C173) is appropriately qualified and supported by cited literature. Claim C174 is a reasonable suggestion for future research directions.

results.result: Aortic and pulmonary IC differ in development: aortic IC develops more proximally without myocardial cuff, while pulmonary IC is more distal and completely surrounded by cardiomyocytes. These differences are also reported in human embryos. Pulmonary IC has less NCC contribution and may have different genetic regulation based on Vangl2 vs Tbx1 mutant differences. IC express tropoelastin during formation while main cushions do not, reflecting lineage differences. These differences may impact morphogenesis and differential pathology predisposition. Bicuspid pulmonary valve is rare alone but common with tetralogy of Fallot, suggesting SHF defects affecting IC development may be relevant to many human valve abnormalities.
results.evaluation: Claims C175-C180 describe well-documented differences between aortic and pulmonary IC supported by the morphological and lineage tracing data. results.result: The four septal valve leaflets are dominated by NCC and EndMT-derived cells, while intercalated leaflets differentiate directly from Tnnt2-Cre+/Isl1+ progenitors via a Notch-Jag dependent mechanism. Disruption of these progenitors causes intercalated leaflet dysplasia and bicuspid valves without raphe, most commonly affecting the aortic valve. This study overturns the dogma that heart valves form principally by EndMT, identifies a new source of valve interstitial cells, and provides a novel mechanism for bicuspid aortic valves without raphe.

results.result: Background on outflow tract and valve development: SHF cells make major contributions to outflow tract walls forming myocardium, smooth muscle, and endocardium. Cardiac jelly prevents retrograde flow and becomes localized to endocardial cushions that are populated by mesenchymal cells. Main outflow cushions receive major NCC contributions while few NCC are in atrioventricular valves. Intercalated cushions give rise to remaining leaflets with only minor NCC contribution. Arterial roots have complex origins from SHF and NCC.
